'''Walter Hendrik Gustav Lewin''' (born January 29, 1936) is a Dutch [[Astrophysics|astrophysicist]] and retired professor of [[physics]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. Lewin earned his doctorate in [[nuclear physics]] in 1965 at the [[Delft University of Technology]] and was a member of MIT's physics faculty for 43 years beginning in 1966 until his retirement in 2009. 

Lewin's contributions in astrophysics include the first discovery of a rotating [[neutron star]] through all-sky balloon surveys and research in X-ray detection in investigations through satellites and observatories. Lewin has received awards for teaching and is known for his lectures on physics and their publication online via [[YouTube]], [[MIT OpenCourseWare]] and [[edX]].

In December 2014, MIT revoked Lewin's Professor Emeritus title after an MIT investigation determined that Lewin had violated university policy by sexually harassing an online student in a [[MITx]] course he had taught.<ref name="Globe_MIT_removes_lectures" /><ref name="Tech_harassment">{{cite news | url= http://tech.mit.edu/V134/N60/walterlewin.html | work= [[The Tech (newspaper)|The Tech]] | title= MIT cuts ties with Walter Lewin after online harassment probe | date= December 9, 2014 | first= Leon | last= Lin | access-date= March 12, 2017 | archive-date= January 9, 2018 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180109034614/http://tech.mit.edu/V134/N60/walterlewin.html | url-status= dead }}</ref><ref name="MIT_harassment">{{cite press release|url=http://newsoffice.mit.edu/2014/lewin-courses-removed-1208 |title=MIT indefinitely removes online physics lectures and courses by Walter Lewin |publisher=MIT News Office | date=December 8, 2014 }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Lewin was born to Walter Simon Lewin and Pieternella Johanna van der Tang in 1936 in [[The Hague]], Netherlands. He was a child when Nazi Germany [[Netherlands in World War II|occupied The Netherlands]] during World War II.<ref name="mit_labor_of_love" /> His paternal grandparents Gustav and Emma Lewin, who were [[Jewish]], were gassed in [[Auschwitz]] on November 19, 1942.<ref name="love_of_physics">{{cite book | last1=Lewin | first1=Walter | last2=Goldstein | first2=Warren | author-link2=Warren Goldstein (professor) | title=For the Love of Physics: From the End of the Rainbow to the Edge of Time – A Journey Through the Wonders of Physics | publisher=Simon and Schuster | date=2011 | isbn=978-1-4391-0827-7 | pages=[https://archive.org/details/forloveofphysics0000lewi/page/11 11&nbsp;12] | url=https://archive.org/details/forloveofphysics0000lewi/page/11 }}</ref><ref>{{cite AV media | people=Walter Lewin | date=May 10, 2020 | title = In Memory of My Family Murdered by the Nazis | type = YouTube video | language = English | url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DwUexUstPEE | access-date = October 20, 2022}}</ref> To protect the family, Lewin's father — who was Jewish, unlike his mother — decided one day to simply leave without telling anyone. His mother was left to raise the children and run a small school she and her husband had started together. After the war ended, his father resurfaced; Lewin describes having a "more or less normal childhood." His parents continued running the school, which he says strongly influenced his love of teaching.<ref name="mit_labor_of_love">{{cite web | url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2011/walter-lewin-lecture-book-0518.html | title=A labor of love | work=MIT News | author= Jennifer Chu | date=May 18, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | title=A New Physics Superstar | url=https://www.usnews.com/education/online-education/articles/2008/01/10/a-new-physics-superstar | work=U.S. News & World Report | date=January 10, 2008 | author =Kim Clark }}</ref>

==Academic career==
Walter Lewin taught high school physics while studying for his PhD, then he went to [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in January 1966 as a [[post-doctoral]] associate, and was appointed an [[assistant professor]]. He was promoted to [[associate professor]] of physics in 1968 and to full professor in 1974.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20090314235106/http://ocw.mit.edu/OcwWeb/web/courses/instructors/lewin/lewin.htm Instructor Profile: Walter Lewin] at MIT OpenCourseWare (archived 2009)</ref>

At MIT, Lewin joined the [[X-ray astronomy]] group and conducted all-sky balloon surveys with [[George W. Clark]]. Through the late seventies, there were about twenty successful balloon flights. These balloon surveys led to the discovery of five new X-ray sources, whose spectra were very different from the X-ray sources discovered during rocket observations. The X-ray flux of these sources was variable. Among them was GX 1+4 whose X-ray flux appeared to be periodic with a period of about 2.4 minutes. This was the first discovery of a slowly rotating neutron star.<ref>{{Cite journal|bibcode=1971ApJ...169L..17L |doi=10.1086/180805 |title=X-Rays from a New Variable Source GX 1+4 |journal=Astrophysical Journal |volume=169 |page=L17 |date=October 1971 |last1=Lewin |first1=Walter H. G. |last2=Ricker |first2=George R. |last3=McClintock |first3=Jeffrey E. }}</ref>

In October 1967 when [[Scorpius X-1]] was observed, an X-ray flare was detected. The flux went up by a factor of about 4 in ten minutes after which it declined again. This was the first detection of X-ray variability observed during the observations. The rockets used by other researchers could not have discovered that the X-ray sources varied on such short time scales because they were only up for several minutes, whereas the balloons could be in the air for many hours.<ref>{{Cite journal|bibcode=1970ApJ...162L.109L |title=Continual Variations in the High-Energy Flux of X-Rays from Scorpius X-1 |journal=Astrophysical Journal |volume=162 |page=L109 |date=November 1970 |doi=10.1086/180635 |last1=Lewin |first1=Walter H. G. |last2=McClintock |first2=Jeffrey E. |last3=Ryckman |first3=Stanley G. |last4=Glass |first4=Ian S. |last5=Smith |first5=William B. }}</ref>

Lewin was co-investigator on the [[Small Astronomy Satellite 3]] (SAS-3) project. He directed the burst observations and discovered several X-ray bursters, among them was the ''rapid burster''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/objects/binaries/rapid_burster_lc.html|title=The Rapid Burster}}</ref> which can produce thousands of X-ray bursts in one day. His group also discovered that the ''rapid burster'' produces two types of bursts and established a classification of bursts as type I (thermonuclear flashes) and type II (accretion flow instabilities).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sci.esa.int/science-e/www/object/index.cfm?fobjectid=42751 |title=ESA Science & Technology: X-ray light curve of the Rapid Burster in a very active Type II burst state |publisher=Sci.esa.int |access-date=2013-04-20}}</ref>

Lewin was co-principal investigator on [[High Energy Astronomy Observatory 1]] HEAO-1 (A4), which has yielded the first all sky catalog at high-energy X rays. With H. Pedersen and J. van Paradijs, Lewin made extensive studies of optical bursts which are associated with X-ray bursts; for X-ray detections they used SAS-3 and the Japanese observatory "[[Hakucho]]". Their combined burst observations demonstrated that the optical bursts are a few seconds delayed relative to the X-ray bursts. This established the size of the [[accretion disc]] surrounding the accreting [[neutron star]]s.

In his search for millisecond X-ray pulsations from low-mass X-ray binaries, in 1984–85 Lewin made guest observations with the European observatory [[EXOSAT]] in collaboration with colleagues from Amsterdam and Garching, Germany. This led to the unexpected discovery of intensity-dependent [[quasi-periodic oscillation]]s (QPO) in the X-ray flux of GX 5-1. During 1989 to 1992, using the Japanese observatory "[[Ginga (satellite)|Ginga]]", Lewin and his co-workers studied the relation between the X-ray spectral state and the radio brightness of several bright low-mass X-ray binaries.<ref>{{Cite journal|bibcode=1991heaa.conf..251L |title=Quasi-periodic oscillations in low-mass X ray binaries |journal=NAS-NRC, High-Energy Astrophysics. American and Soviet Perspectives |pages=251 |last1=Lewin |first1=Walter H. G. |last2=Van Paradijs |first2=J. |last3=Van Der Klis |first3=M. |year=1991 }}</ref>

Lewin was closely involved in [[ROSAT]] observations of the nearby galaxies [[Andromeda Galaxy|M31]] and [[Messier 81]]. Lewin and his graduate student Eugene Magnier have made deep optical [[charge-coupled device]] observations of M31 in four colors; they have published a catalogue of 500,000 objects. Lewin and his graduate student David Pooley initiated the successful X-ray observations within six days of the appearance of supernova SN 1993J in M81.

Lewin collaborated with his close friend [[Jan van Paradijs]] of the [[University of Amsterdam]] from 1978 until van Paradijs' death. They co-authored 150 papers.<ref>{{cite conference | arxiv=astro-ph/0105344 |title=My Quarter Century with Jan | date = 2003 | author=Walter H. G. Lewin | volume=308 | pages=27 | editor= Edward P. van den Heuvel | editor2= Lex Kaper | editor3= Evert Rol| editor4= Ralph A.M.J. Wijers | conference=ASP Conference Proceedings | bibcode=2003ASPC..308...27L}}</ref>

He became a corresponding member of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1993<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/correspondents/4469 |title=Walter Lewin |publisher=Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences |access-date=17 July 2015 |archive-date=20 July 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150720232059/https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/correspondents/4469 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1993.<ref name="schuster_bio">{{cite web | url=http://authors.simonandschuster.co.uk/Walter-Lewin/49822352 | title=Walter Lewin | work=Simon & Schuster UK | access-date=2015-02-22}}</ref>

Lewin and graduate student Jeffrey Kommers have worked on data from the [[Compton Gamma Ray Observatory]] (GRO). This was a collaboration with the BATSE Group<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.batse.msfc.nasa.gov/batse/instrument/ |title=BATSE-GRO Project |website=www.batse.msfc.nasa.gov |access-date=12 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130215053749/http://www.batse.msfc.nasa.gov/batse/instrument/ |archive-date=15 February 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref> in Huntsville, AL. In early December 1995, with co-workers [[Chryssa Kouveliotou]] and Van Paradijs, they discovered a new type of X-ray burst source: (GRO J1744-28) the [[Bursting Pulsar]], and received a NASA Achievement Award for this discovery.

In 1996–1998, Lewin's collaboration with [[Michiel van der Klis]] in Amsterdam led to the discovery of kHz oscillations in many [[X-ray binary|X-ray binaries]].

Using the [[Chandra X-ray Observatory]], Lewin and his graduate student David Pooley made extensive studies of supernovae and faint X-ray sources in [[globular cluster]]s. This research was done in collaboration with scientists from the [[University of Washington]], [[Institute for Advanced Study|IAS]] in Princeton, [[UC Berkeley]], the [[University of Amsterdam]] and [[Utrecht]] in The Netherlands, and the [[Naval Research Laboratory]] in Washington, DC. The research on [[supernova]]e produced the first X-ray spectrum with unprecedented energy resolution of SN 1989S.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pooley|first1=David|last2=Lewin|first2=Walter H. G.|last3=Verbunt|first3=Frank|last4=Homer|first4=Lee|last5=Margon|first5=Bruce|last6=Gaensler|first6=Bryan M.|last7=Kaspi|first7=Victoria M.|last8=Miller|first8=Jon M.|last9=Fox|first9=Derek W.|date=28 March 2002|title=Chandra Observation of the Globular Cluster NGC 6440 and the Nature of Cluster X-ray Luminosity Functions|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|volume=573|issue=1|pages=184–190|doi=10.1086/340498|issn=0004-637X|arxiv=astro-ph/0111212|bibcode=2002ApJ...573..184P|s2cid=119401055}}</ref> The research on [[globular cluster]]s demonstrated that X-ray binary stars are cooked in the cores of the clusters where the [[stellar density]] is very high.

With graduate student Jon Miller, Lewin made extensive studies of [[X-ray binary|black-hole X-ray binaries]] in the galaxy. Evidence was found for [[Log-spectral distance|spectral distortions]] of the [[Broad iron K line|iron line]] (in X-rays) indicative of the influence of [[general relativity]] on the iron-line emission in the vicinity of the "[[event horizon]]" of the [[black hole]]s. This research on black-hole binaries is continuing using all available observatories in orbit – among them: [[Chandra X-ray Observatory|Chandra]], the [[Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer]] (RXTE), and the European observatories [[XMM-Newton]], [[Integral]] and [[NuSTAR]].

Lewin has published about 450 scientific articles as of 2014.<ref name="schuster_bio" />

===Lectures===
For about 15 years (starting in 1982) Lewin presented a one-hour program weekly on MIT Cable TV. The shows were aired 24 hours per day helping freshmen with their weekly homework assignments. Videos of Lewin's lectures on Newtonian mechanics (1999), electricity and magnetism (2002) and the physics of vibrations and waves (2004), among others, could be viewed on the MIT OpenCourseWare web site until MIT removed them after finding that Lewin had sexually harassed a student in the online course.<ref name="MIT_harassment" />

Since February 2015, Lewin has been running and managing his own YouTube channel called "Lectures by Walter Lewin. They will make you ♥ Physics".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lectures by Walter Lewin. They will make you ♥ Physics. - YouTube |url=https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCiEHVhv0SBMpP75JbzJShqw/ |website=[[YouTube]]}}</ref> Several of his lectures have been viewed more than a million times. His 2011 farewell lecture "For the Love of Physics" has been viewed around 15 million times - 1 million times on MIT's OCW, 6.9 million times on the channel "For the Allure of Physics"<ref name="sati8335">{{cite news | url=https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCliSRiiRVQuDfgxI_QN_Fmw/videos | title= YouTube Channel Containing Lewin's Video Lectures | date=March 25, 2015 | author=sati8335}}</ref> and 6.9 million times on his personal channel.<ref>Archived at [https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211205/sJG-rXBbmCc Ghostarchive]{{cbignore}} and the [https://web.archive.org/web/20150827153837/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sJG-rXBbmCc Wayback Machine]{{cbignore}}: {{cite web| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sJG-rXBbmCc| title = For the Love of Physics - Walter Lewin - May 16, 2011 | website=[[YouTube]]| date = 11 February 2015 }}{{cbignore}}</ref> In 2007, a picture of Lewin swinging on a pendulum during a lecture at MIT, was shown on the front page of the New York Times "At 71, Professor is a Pendulum and a Web Star".<ref name=":2">{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/12/19/education/19physics.html?_r=1&hp&oref=slogin | title=At 71, Physics Professor is Web Star | work=The New York Times | author=Sara Rimer | date=December 19, 2007}}</ref>

==Sexual harassment==
In early December 2014, MIT determined that Lewin had sexually harassed an online [[MITx]] learner, in violation of MIT's policies.<ref name="Globe_MIT_removes_lectures">{{cite news | work=[[The Boston Globe]] | url=http://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2014/12/09/mit-removes-online-lectures-popular-retired-professor-after-sexual-harassment-charge/cbHVoxUCWd1YRKbpJw8rfL/story.html | title=MIT removes professor's online lectures after harassment charge | date=December 9, 2014 | first=Juan Esteban | last=Cajigas Jimenez | url-status=bot: unknown | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141209071205/http://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2014/12/09/mit-removes-online-lectures-popular-retired-professor-after-sexual-harassment-charge/cbHVoxUCWd1YRKbpJw8rfL/story.html | archive-date=December 9, 2014 }}</ref> ''[[Inside Higher Ed]]'' reported that this learner was one of at least 10 female students to whom Lewin had sent inappropriate messages, which MIT confirmed.<ref name="insidehighered">{{cite news | url=https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2015/01/23/complainant-unprecedented-walter-lewin-sexual-harassment-case-comes-forward | work=Inside Higher Ed | title=We All Felt Trapped | date=January 23, 2015 | first=Carl |last= Straumsheim |access-date= March 12, 2017}}</ref> The woman came forward to ensure that the case was not forgotten, stating that Lewin pushed her to participate in sexual role-playing and asked for sexually explicit photos.<ref name="insidehighered" /> As a consequence of its internal investigation, MIT revoked Lewin's [[professor emeritus]] title,<ref name="Tech_harassment"/> and removed his lectures from the institute's online learning platforms.<ref name="Tech_14Jan2015">{{cite news | work=The Tech | url=http://tech.mit.edu/V134/N62/lewin.html | title=MIT says it removed Lewin videos for fear of continued harassment | date=January 14, 2015 | first=Leon | last=Lin | access-date=April 14, 2015 | archive-date=July 11, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150711053126/http://tech.mit.edu/V134/N62/lewin.html | url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Lewin is an art enthusiast and collector. He has lectured on the subject at MIT.<ref>Lewin, Walter (date unknown). "Walter Lewin: Looking at 20th Century Art through the Eyes of a Physicist". Retrieved from https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCiEHVhv0SBMpP75JbzJShqw.</ref> In the 1970s and 1980s, he collaborated with the artist [[Otto Piene]], who was one of the founders of the [[Zero (art)|ZERO movement]] and the director of MIT's [[Center for Advanced Visual Studies]],<ref>{{cite news | title= Otto Piene, leading figure in kinetic and technology-based art, dies at 86 | work=MIT News | date=July 21, 2014 | author=Val Grimm | url=http://newsoffice.mit.edu/2014/otto-piene-leading-figure-kinetic-and-technology-based-art-dies-86}}</ref> and [[Peter Struycken]], who is a [[computer art]]ist.<ref name="love_of_physics" />
